title: Foundry stales 20 full-difficulty Bitcoin blocks that no observer saw
summary: Across September 11 and 12, 2025, Foundry USA produced 20 full-difficulty Bitcoin blocks at 16 heights (914,261 to 914,373) that all went stale, foregoing roughly 46.9 BTC. No public fork observer holds a record of them; the evidence survives only in RSK and Fractal AuxPoW captures.
body:
It began with a self-race: at height `914,261` on September 11, Foundry staled a block against its own canonical winner. About three and a half hours later the cluster proper started, and over roughly 17 hours Foundry staled 19 more full-difficulty blocks at 15 further heights, through `914,373`. Thirteen of the twenty carry Foundry's coinbase tags directly; the other seven are tied to Foundry through the RSK reward-address registry on their AuxPoW evidence. The 15 height races lost to competing pools put the foregone reward at roughly 46.9 BTC in subsidy plus fees.[^1]

The timing profile points at the pool layer rather than a propagation race. Within the cluster, the stale headers carry timestamps 6 to 1,621 seconds earlier than their canonical winners (median about 600 seconds). Header clocks are self-reported and are not observation times, so they cannot prove which block was found first; what they do show is Foundry repeatedly stamping templates well before the blocks that beat them. Each stale builds on a canonical parent and none chain onto each other, the signature of a recurring failure in the block-submission path rather than a chain split.[^1]

No public record of these blocks exists outside merge mining. ForkMonitor and its peers hold nothing for them, and a fork observer only captures a stale that one of its own nodes saw in real time; Bitcoin keeps no durable network-wide stale record. The strongest available statement from observers alone is that if these blocks propagated at all, nobody watching recorded it; taken together with the timing profile, the most plausible reading is an internal failure at the pool, blocks assembled and stamped that never propagated to the network.[^2] The episode is visible today only because merge-mined child chains embed every Bitcoin parent template they see: the RSK and Fractal captures preserved all 20 headers. Foundry later left merge mining entirely in June 2026, closing the channel that made this incident observable.

figures.accessible_summary: Twenty discrete Foundry stale blocks occurred from September 11 to 12. Nineteen form a 17-hour cluster. Header-time deficits range from 6 to 1,621 seconds, with a median of 577.5 seconds across all twenty values.
figures.note: One discrete mark per stale block from this monitor's competition data, queried 2026-07-29. Header clocks are self-reported, not observation times.
